title: British TV Sector Revenues Hit $5.1 Billion Last Year Driven by U.S. Streamers: It ‘Underlines the Strength of the U.K. Production Market’
description:
British TV sector revenues hit £3.81 billion ($5.1 billion) last year, largely driven by U.S. streamers.

	The results were published by Pact, the U
body:
British TV sector revenues hit £3.81 billion ($5.1 billion) last year, largely driven by U.S. streamers.

	The results were published by Pact, the U.K. producers trade group, who noted the figure represented a £149 million (4.1%) increase on 2024 revenues. They say it is driven primarily by streaming investment into the U.K.

	International TV revenue accounted for 41.1% of total revenue in 2025, a figure of £1.57 billion, an increase of £214 million (15.8%) year-on-year. It is the first time the figure has grown since the post-Covid rebound 2022.
	

	Pact noted that SVOD platforms such as Netflix, makers of “The Gentlemen” and “Black Doves,” and Amazon’s Prime Video, who boast “Clarkson’s Farm” and “L.O.L. Last One Laughing U.K.,” have continued to grow their commissioning budgets, resulting in all-time high investment into the country.


	Conversely, however, revenues from domestic TV have fallen below £2 billion for the first time in five years (a 4.7% drop year on year) driven by a drop in U.K. commissions. Pact put this down to a small decline in spend from public service broadcasters such as the BBC and ITV and a “larger decline” in multichannel spend.

	While international commissions accounted for 35% of all primary commissions, U.K. PSB network commissions decreased dropped from by 10% to 58%.

	However £1.42 billion – at 85.9% the majority of revenue — still comes via PSB commissions.

	According to Pact’s data producers are becoming increasingly canny about diversifying, with non-TV revenue growing by £34 million last year thanks to U.K. feature films, management and event production and advertising, among other revenue streams. Secondary rights revenue also grew by 12.7% to a record £575 million.
	

	“Pact’s 2026 census underlines once again the strength of the U.K. production market in attracting inward investment, but also its vulnerability to declining domestic spend,” said Pact CEO, Nigel Warner.

	“While it is welcome to see the proportion of investment in the nations and regions holding up, it is concerning that the pressures on new and smaller indies remain acute. A new settlement for a strong and sustainable BBC is urgently needed. The entrepreneurial spirit continues to drive the U.K.’s independent sector’s success, but we need to see growth in domestic PSB investment to help all parts of the production sector to thrive.”

schema.headline: British TV Sector Revenues Hit $5.1 Billion Last Year Driven by U.S. Streamers: It ‘Underlines the Strength of the U.K. Production Market’

title: John Malkovich Drops Out of ‘The Music Critic’ in Israel After Press Release Attributed False Quotes
description: John Malkovich has pulled out of a performance of “The Music Critic” set to take place in Tel Aviv, Israel, after a press release falsely attributed
body:
John Malkovich has pulled out of a performance of “The Music Critic” set to take place in Tel Aviv, Israel, after a press release falsely attributed quotes to the actor.

	“I was made aware of an article which appeared in The Hollywood Reporter (first published in The Jerusalem Post) announcing a date in Tel Aviv, Israel, for a performance of a piece called ‘The Music Critic,’ one of the numerous classical music collaborations and live theatre performances I have been touring in for nearly two decades and which I have performed in 47 countries at last count. The Tel Aviv date was meant to be one of several touring stops throughout Europe and the Middle East,” Malkovich said in a statement.
	

	He continued: “A PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed. I did not utter these phrases, and they most certainly are not approved by me, nor do they reflect my feelings. The fact that they were printed as direct quotes from me is unacceptable and untenable. For this reason, I have decided I cannot participate in the Tel Aviv performance.” 


	In a correction now posted to the initial story, The Jerusalem Post wrote that “Alon Yurick, the show’s Israeli producer, clarified that the original press release contained an incorrect quote resulting from a misunderstanding and apologized for the error.” The Jerusalem Post has since removed Malkovich’s fabricated quote.

	In his statement, the actor also noted that his appearance in a country “does not constitute approval of said country’s policies, nor actions, nor its elected or unelected leaders.” “My appearances would also not condone nor mean that I am in supposed ‘solidarity’ with any particular political cause, nor with the killing of innocents, nor with any acts of terrorism, nor any other kind of barbarity,” he added. 
	

	Before Malkovich decided to drop out, the performance was scheduled for April 13, 2027, at the Charles Bronfman Auditorium. “The Music Critic” was created and conceived by violinist and composer Aleksey Igudesman.

	Read Malkovich’s full statement here:

	I was made aware of an article which appeared in The Hollywood Reporter (first published in The Jerusalem Post) announcing a date in Tel Aviv, Israel, for a performance of a piece called ‘The Music Critic,’ one of the numerous classical music collaborations and live theatre performances I have been touring in for nearly two decades and which I have performed in 47 countries at last count. The Tel Aviv date was meant to be one of several touring stops throughout Europe and the Middle East.

	A PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed. I did not utter these phrases, and they most certainly are not approved by me, nor do they reflect my feelings. The fact that they were printed as direct quotes from me is unacceptable and untenable. For this reason, I have decided I cannot participate in the Tel Aviv performance.

	Throughout my long career, I’ve been lucky to perform across a quite wide swath of the world— in countries with governments whose values or culture I do not share and in front of audiences of many differing faiths and ideologies. Traveling to places whose view of the world may not align with mine has given me a chance to observe and to listen and learn and to share my idea of what makes good storytelling and what makes beautiful music and how they can complement each other and illuminate the human condition. 

	My appearance in any country, even my own, does not constitute approval of said country’s policies, nor actions, nor its elected or unelected leaders. My appearances would also not condone nor mean that I am in supposed “solidarity” with any particular political cause, nor with the killing of innocents, nor with any acts of terrorism, nor any other kind of barbarity. Generally speaking, I believe that we need more culture and more beauty in more places, not less. Art, at its best, reminds us that the exercise of our shared humanity can and should be a tool to bridge our conflicts and our griefs, our grievances and our sorrows, and that the exercise of artistic freedom is often the greatest form of protest against savagery. I look forward to continuing to exercise my artistic freedom, come what may. However, only playwrights, novelists and screenwriters can put words in my mouth, and even then, only in the service of storytelling, and no one else should think they can do that without my consent and without the resultant consequences.

schema.headline: John Malkovich Drops Out of ‘The Music Critic’ in Israel After Press Release Attributed False Quotes

title: John Mulaney Circling Lead Role in ‘Get Smart’ Reboot at Warner Bros.
description:
John Mulaney is circling the role of Agent Maxwell Smart in Warner Bros. upcoming movie reboot of “Get Smart,” Variety has confirmed.

	The project
body:
John Mulaney is circling the role of Agent Maxwell Smart in Warner Bros. upcoming movie reboot of “Get Smart,” Variety has confirmed.

	The project is still in very early stages. Seth Grahame-Smith, who wrote 2025’s “Now You See Me: Now You Don’t,” is set to pen the screenplay. Producers include Andrew Lazar and Chuck Roven.

	Co-creators Mel Brooks and Buck Henry debuted the original “Get Smart” TV series in 1965, and it ran for 138 episodes until 1970. Don Adams led the slapstick spy spoof as the brainy but hopelessly incompetent Agent Smart, starring alongside Barbara Feldon as the ever-capable Agent 99. Edward Platt played the Chief of the Control agency. “Get Smart” earned seven Emmy wins during its run, including three acting wins for Adams and three for Outstanding Comedy Series.
	

	“Get Smart” was first adapted for the big screen in 2008, with Steve Carell in the titular role. Anne Hathaway, Dwayne Johnson, Alan Arkin and Terence Stamp co-starred. Directed by “50 First Dates” filmmaker Peter Segal, the film was a moderate success, opening to $38 million and earning $230 million worldwide by the end of its run against a budget of $80 million (not adjusted for inflation).


	Mulaney’s most recent starring role was as the host of Netflix’s anti-talk show “Everybody’s Live with John Mulaney,” which had a 12-episode run in 2025. He has a nine-show New York comedy tour, “Mulaney Takes Manhattan,” set to kick off in January. His next movie role will be in David O. Russell’s sports biopic “Madden” as Trip Hawkins, the founder of the video game giant Electronic Arts.
	

	Mulaney joked during the 2024 Governors Awards that he auditioned for the role of “Young Cop” in Maggie Gyllenhaal’s “The Bride!,” which was a Warner Bros. release. Now it looks like the four-time Emmy winner and WB. are finally coming together.

schema.headline: John Mulaney Circling Lead Role in ‘Get Smart’ Reboot at Warner Bros.

title: Netflix Orders New Series Take On ‘Lonesome Dove’ From ‘East of Eden’ Showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart
description: “Lonesome Dove,” which was originally adapted into an Emmy- and Golden Globe-winning CBS miniseries starring Robert Duvall in 1989, is getting a new
body:
“Lonesome Dove,” which was originally adapted into an Emmy- and Golden Globe-winning CBS miniseries starring Robert Duvall in 1989, is getting a new take at Netflix. The streamer announced Tuesday that it had ordered “Lonesome Dove” to series, from co-showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart.

	Kazan and Stuart are also the co-showrunners on Netflix’s upcoming limited series “East of Eden.” Kazan and Stuart were hired by Teton Ridge Entertainment, which holds the rights to “Lonesome Dove,” the Pulitzer Prize-winning western novel from author Larry McMurtry first released in 1985. The CBS miniseries was a smash, attracting 26 million viewers and spawned multiple sequels (“Return to Lonesome Dove,” “Streets of Laredo,” “Dead Man’s Walk,” “Comanche Moon”) as well as the 1994 syndicated “Lonesome Dove: The Series.”
	

	Here’s the logline: “Gus McCrae and Woodrow Call renew their spirit of adventure as they face an uncertain future, embarking on one final, perilous cattle drive from the Rio Grande to the untamed wilderness of Montana in pursuit of a dream that they have perhaps already outlived. These two former Texas Rangers lead an unforgettable cast of characters across the American west in this sweeping odyssey defined by unrequited longing, unbreakable friendship, brutal frontier justice, and an unwavering pursuit of a meaningful life.”


	Teton Ridge acquired the rights to “Lonesome Dove” last year; at the time, it announced that development would begin with the first book in the series, “Lonesome Dove,” followed by the rest of the tetralogy, including “Streets of Laredo,” “Dead Man’s Walk” and “Comanche Moon.” The novels focus on members of the Texas Ranger Division, spanning from when Texas was a republic until the start of the 20th century when it was part of the U.S.
	

	Kazan and Stuart will serve as co-showrunners/writers/executive producers, while EPs also include Thomas Tull, Jillian Share and Jen Gorton of Teton Ridge Entertainment; Jon Jashni; Diana Ossana; and Curtis McMurtry of the McMurtry Estate. Diana Ossana, McMurty’s longtime creative partner, is also an exec producer.

	“’Lonesome Dove’ is one of the great American stories, and there was no question we wanted to follow Zoe and Jeb wherever they went next,” said Netflix head of scripted series, U.S. and Canada, Jinny Howe. “After ‘East of Eden,’ we know exactly what they’re capable of — the depth of character, the sweep of place, the emotional precision. This material deserves that level of care. In their hands, it’s going to be something extraordinary. We’re excited to partner with Teton Ridge to bring this legendary story to life.”

	In a joint statement, Kazan and Stuart said that “we come to this material with love and respect, and can’t wait to hit the trail with Gus and Call and the rest of these beloved characters.” And Teton Ridge Entertainment president Jillian Share added: “‘Lonesome Dove’ is the kind of story that only comes along once in a generation. Its characters, scope and deeply human portrait of the American West have made it an enduring classic, and we see an extraordinary opportunity to bring Larry McMurtry’s world to a new generation of audiences.”

	Said Ossana: “‘Lonesome Dove’ has been part of my creative life for decades, an important part of Larry’s and my partnership journey. Its characters, landscape, and profound understanding of friendship, love, loss, and human longing have stayed with me, and it is deeply meaningful to help bring this newly imagined, extraordinary world of ‘Lonesome Dove’ to a contemporary generation while preserving the emotional truths that make all of Larry’s work timeless.”

schema.headline: Netflix Orders New Series Take On ‘Lonesome Dove’ From ‘East of Eden’ Showrunners Zoe Kazan and Jeb Stuart

title: Louis Messina, Taylor Swift’s Tour Promoter, Urges Judge to Reject Live Nation/Ticketmaster Antitrust Settlement: ‘I Could Go Out of Business Like Other Promoters Who Have Fallen Victim to Live Nation’
description: You might think that the man who promoted Taylor Swift‘s Eras Tour, as well as all of her other global outings, would be powerful enough not to feel
body:
You might think that the man who promoted Taylor Swift‘s Eras Tour, as well as all of her other global outings, would be powerful enough not to feel intimidated by Live Nation and Ticketmaster. Yet Louis Messina wrote in a submission to a federal judge that he, too, is vulnerable to the company wielding its power as part of its alleged monopoly, urging the judge presiding over the case to reject a consent decree now under consideration that would let the company stay intact.
	

	“I write this letter because I am concerned that the music industry is broken. If it is not fixed, I could go out of business just like other independent promoters who have fallen victim to Live Nation,” the Messina Touring Group CEO wrote. “The jury verdict in this case is a step in the right direction and will give the court an opportunity to try to reign in Live Nation’s conduct. But the consent decree is a step backward—it does not fix the industry and likely would make things worse.”


	He further suggested that he is speaking up because he has less to lose than other promoters who are in a much more vulnerable position going up against Live Nation. Messina Group’s artists include stadium-fillers like Kenny Chesney, George Strait and Ed Sheeran as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Eric Church, Zac Brown Band and Blake Shelton.

	“Most artists, agents, and managers are afraid of speaking out against Live Nation because they could lose everything if Live Nation turns against them. Live Nation already has turned against me,” wrote Messina, CEO of Messina Touring Company, in a statement aligning himself with AEG and alleging he has  been discriminated against because of his association with the rival group. He claimed that Live Nation stopped even returning his calls in 2024 and only resumed communicating with him this year.
	

	In the letter, Messina said that he was “trying to route several tours through Live Nation amphitheaters, but Live Nation stopped returning my calls,” Messina wrote. The promoter says being allegedly shut out of Live Nation venues adversely affected his ability to work with several clients, including the Lumineers, Old Dominion and Shawn Mendes, as well as potential client Mumford & Sons, which he says had to use Live Nation as a promoter to get into Live Nation-owned ampthitheaters.

	“If Live Nation prohibits artists from using me to promote their amphitheater shows, I cannot compete,” Messina wrote.

	“The first problem is Live Nation’s monopoly money. Live Nation does not make its money by promoting tours and helping artists,” Messina wrote. “Instead, Live Nation makes its money from ticketing fees and sponsorships. You can look at their public financial statements. Live Nation makes almost a billion dollars from ticketing fees every year while in many years they make little, if any money in their touring business. What does that mean? It means that Live Nation can throw monopoly money at artists in the form of big guarantees—more money than any other promoter can offer. Live Nation does not even care if a tour loses money because they are making a billion dollars on the massive ticketing fees. As a result, Live Nation has either bought or driven out of business most of the independent promoters in this country.”

	Things have gone both for and against Live Nation and Ticketmaster in the legal sphere this year. The federal government’s proposed consent decree looked to keep the company safe from a breakup, but some states who were joining the action refused to join in the settlement, and a jury found Live Nation liable on some of the original antitrust claims.

	Wrote Messina, “For many years, I was able to help artists like Taylor Swift and Kenny Chesney develop their careers by promoting tours in Live Nation amphitheaters before they developed the fan base to headline their own tours in larger venues. All artists must start somewhere, and I am right there with the artists when they start. For more than two decades, I have been able to promote artists in Live Nation amphitheaters. It was critical to my artists and to the survival of my business.
	

	“But my artists’ situation was unique. Live Nation blocked other artists from using their amphitheaters unless they also used Live Nation to promote their tour. But my arrangement with Live Nation ended in 2024. I was trying to route several tours through Live Nation amphitheaters, but Live Nation stopped returning my calls. Ultimately none of the artists were able to use the promoter they wanted. For example, Old Dominion was forced to route through other venues and the tour underperformed because they could not play Live Nation amphitheaters. Live Nation agreed to let the Lumineers play in the amphitheaters, but only if I was not involved. Shawn Mendes’ agent also had to negotiate directly with Live Nation because Live Nation was not returning my calls. I was in discussions to promote Mumford & Sons, but the band was forced to use Live Nation because that was the only way they could access Live Nation’s amphitheaters. Similarly, when I spoke with Parker McCollum and his team, their first question was, ‘What about the amphitheaters?’ That question captured my dire situation. If Live Nation prohibits artists from using me to promote their amphitheater shows, I cannot compete. I will not be able to help developing artists build their careers.

	“Live Nation began returning my calls again in 2026 after the consent decree was submitted. I do not know whether I will be able to get the dates and terms I need to promote shows at Live Nation amphitheaters. But what I experienced in 2024 drove home how easy it is for Live Nation to destroy my business, like it has destroyed other promoters, and how something needs to change or Live Nation will always be able to hold the industry hostage. The consent decree does not solve the amphitheater problem.”

	Live Nation did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Messina’s letter.

schema.headline: Louis Messina, Taylor Swift’s Tour Promoter, Urges Judge to Reject Live Nation/Ticketmaster Antitrust Settlement: ‘I Could Go Out of Business Like Other Promoters Who Have Fallen Victim to Live Nation’

title: Fired ‘60 Minutes’ Managing Editor Says New CBS Bosses Wanted ‘White House Talking Points in Our Reporting’ and ‘We Questioned Authority’
description: Former “60 Minutes” managing editor Guy Campanile, who was fired in May alongside some top correspondents, has spoken out about his sudden ouster fr
body:
Former “60 Minutes” managing editor Guy Campanile, who was fired in May alongside some top correspondents, has spoken out about his sudden ouster from the venerable CBS News program.

	In a private Facebook post obtained by The Guardian and recirculated by reporter Justin Baragona, Campanile wrote that “after some time and deep reflection,” he is “now comfortable and prepared to talk about” his exit. Campanile, who worked at CBS News for 34 years, said he and his former colleagues — including fired correspondents Scott Pelley and Sharyn Alfonsi, to name a couple — “refused to be accomplices in the destruction of the most prestigious news program on American television.”
	

	“We would not compromise our principles or reputations by jamming unverifiable notions or White House talking points into our reporting,” Campanile continued. “We objected when told to conduct interviews arranged by the administration. We insisted on asking the most challenging questions to business and political leaders without fear or favor. We did what reporters worth their salt do — we questioned authority … including our own bosses. That’s how the best newsrooms work. To be clear — we were told to leave because we insisted on doing our jobs.”


	CBS did not immediately respond to Variety‘s request for comment.

	The long-running newsmagazine has faced scandals, internal dissent and media backlash ever since CBS News was taken over by Paramount Skydance and the Ellison family, which installed Free Press founder Bari Weiss as editorial chief. Many former “60 Minutes” staffers have spoken out against the new regime, with Pelley alleging editorial decisions were made to “curry favor with the Trump administration” and “good people were silenced because they stood up for our audience” and “fairness against the forces of political bias.”
	

	In his lengthy Facebook post, Campanile echoed many of Pelley’s concerns. “What has happened recently at ’60 Minutes’ – where I believe editorial independence has become a casualty of corporate priorities and ideological intrusion – was tragic,” he wrote. “But it was part of an inevitable progression in the cascade of afflictions that have devalued our most trusted sources of news.”

	He issued the statement the same day “60 Minutes” teased its new season (premiering on Sept. 13) with a photo of its lineup of correspondents, including mainstays Lesley Stahl and Bill Whitaker alongside newcomers Norah O’Donnell and Ross Douthat.

	Without naming names, Campanile criticized the ways in which information has become “commoditized in the attention economy.” “Making matters worse is the cadre of self-described influencers and on-line opinionists who market themselves as ‘journalists,'” he wrote. “Some have been given control of our most precious reporting institutions — including CBS News.”

	Campanile concluded his remarks by saying he left CBS News “with my head held high and integrity intact.” 

	“I am excited about the opportunities ahead. In the meantime, I cannot remain silent as trust built over decades by my colleagues and mentors is wrecked,” he wrote. “The audience deserves so much better. Thomas Jefferson wrote, ‘Our liberty depends on the freedom of the press, and that cannot be limited without being lost.’ It’s dangerous to ignore his warning. As for my friends that remain at my former employer: Hold the line. Don’t give an inch because they will keep scraping away until there’s nothing left worth a damn.”

	While Campanile did not mention specific incidents at “60 Minutes,” Pelley previously said “new management has instructed me to inject falsehoods and bias into a politically sensitive story” and that “recently, politicians have been invited to choose correspondents for interviews.” Last year, a segment about the “horrific treatment” of detainees deported from the U.S. to a prison in El Salvador was yanked by Weiss a few hours before airtime. Weiss said the segment “wasn’t ready,” while correspondents pushed back against their new boss, with Alfonsi claiming Weiss’ interference was “not an editorial decision, it is a political one.”

schema.headline: Fired ‘60 Minutes’ Managing Editor Says New CBS Bosses Wanted ‘White House Talking Points in Our Reporting’ and ‘We Questioned Authority’

title: Congress Begins Drafting 20% Federal Film Incentive With Trump’s Blessing (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Members of Congress are drafting legislation that would create a 20% federal film and TV incentive — with bonuses that could bring it as high as 30%
body:
Members of Congress are drafting legislation that would create a 20% federal film and TV incentive — with bonuses that could bring it as high as 30% — after President Trump endorsed the idea last week.

	The bill is expected to be introduced this month, and perhaps as soon as the end of next week, according to sources familiar with the process. Rep. Nathaniel Moran, a Republican from East Texas, is working on the bill with Rep. Linda Sanchez, a Democrat from Whittier, Calif. Both serve on the House Ways and Means Committee, which is responsible for tax legislation.
	

	Rep. Laura Friedman, a Democrat from Burbank, Calif., has also been working with Rep. Brian Jack, a Republican from the Atlanta suburbs, on the bipartisan effort.


	For the last year, the Motion Picture Association and entertainment unions have been advocating for an incentive that would compete with generous subsidies from the U.K., Canada, Australia and scores of other countries. Trump threw his weight behind the idea in a Truth Social post on Aug. 31, a development expected to unlock Republican support on Capitol Hill.

	The draft legislation broadly aligns with the MPA’s request. The bill would offer a base credit of 20% of all labor costs, both below-the-line and above-the-line. A wide range of productions would be eligible, including reality TV and animation in addition to films and scripted TV shows, according to sources familiar with the legislation. It would not include news or sports broadcasts.

	The bill would also include four “uplifts” meant to attract political support. According to a source, the bill would allow producers to claim an additional five percent if they meet one of these four criteria:
	


film in a rural opportunity zone
make an independent production
bring a certain amount of filming back to the U.S. from abroad
spend at least $10 million in 10 different states in a year



	Producers could claim up to two of those uplifts, for a maximum of 30%. The federal tax credit would stack on top of state incentives, meaning that productions could see a total subsidy of 60% or more depending on where they film. 

	Supporters have argued that the incentive will not just help Los Angeles and New York — where the bulk of production takes place — but will also boost rural areas that currently have little filming and little or no state tax incentive. 

	The hope is that spreading production around will broaden support, much the way the state incentives in California and New York attracted votes from rural lawmakers by offering a bonus for filming outside of Los Angeles and New York City, respectively.

	California lawmakers have also pushed for a bonus for any production in an area that was recently declared a federal disaster zone. (All of Los Angeles County would qualify due to the 2025 fires.) That is not included in the latest draft.

	The tax credit could be used to offset federal income tax, or be sold to another taxpayer to offset their tax liability. It would not be refundable.

	The bill has yet to go to the Joint Committee on Taxation, which will get a score on how much it would cost — though it is safe to say it will run into the billions of dollars. In his post last week, Trump argued that the cost would be “made up tenfold by the money pouring into the Treasury’s coffers.”

	The MPA is expected to issue a report in the coming weeks that would expound on that claim, arguing that production creates a ripple effect that benefits the local economy. 

	Some supporters of the measure are optimistic about getting it through Congress as part of a tax bill during the lame duck session after the November election, though it may be more likely to happen next year.

	“I would be very happy for it to happen in the lame duck,” Friedman said in an interview last week. “I can’t promise that’s possible. We’re going to try not only to get this done quickly, but to have all our ducks in a row.”

	Friedman said that the discussions took on a new momentum after Trump got involved.

	“I can’t tell you the number of texts that have come in from people who have offered to help,” she said.
	

	She declined to discuss the specifics of the legislation, but said she is working to build a coalition across the country behind the idea.

	“Everyone in every state loves movies and television,” she said. “Everyone benefits by this product being made here.”

schema.headline: Congress Begins Drafting 20% Federal Film Incentive With Trump’s Blessing (EXCLUSIVE)

title: Bruce Davis, Longtime AMPAS Executive Director, Dies at 83
description: Bruce Davis, who served as Executive Director of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and helped develop the Margaret Herrick Library and
body:
Bruce Davis, who served as Executive Director of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and helped develop the Margaret Herrick Library and Academy Film Archive, died Sept. 5 in Los Angeles. He was 83.

	Davis came to the Academy after chairing the theater department at Juniata College in Pennsylvania. He started out at the Academy overseeing public programming, and was named Executive Director in 1989. He retired from the Academy in 2011. 
	

	His tenure included two major achievements in film preservation: Davis worked with the city of Beverly Hills and Academy president Robert Wise to acquire rights to the 1928 building that became the Margaret Herrick Library, and oversaw the acquisition of the 1948 television studio in Hollywood that became the Academy Film Archive. 


	After retiring, Davis published the book “The Academy and the Award” about the origins and history of the Oscars. 

	He was known at the Academy for his wit, his writing skills and his Friday Lunch tradition where staff members from various departments would join him to eat and converse.

	Born in Washington D.C., he became a film buff at a young age. At Juniata College, he founded the film department and led the theater department, as well as studying filmmaking at Columbia University. 

	He is survived by his wife Joann and four daughters: Brangien Davis (Daniel Spils); Alexandra Davis; Archer Davis (Tom Brown) and Roxanne Davis. 

	Donations may be made to Juniata College.

schema.headline: Bruce Davis, Longtime AMPAS Executive Director, Dies at 83

title: Telluride Takeaways: From Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti’s ‘Debut’ to Nathan Fielder’s Audacious Dare to the Doc Branch
description: On my last morning in Telluride, halfway through breakfast at Butcher & Baker, Kenneth Branagh stopped at the table on his way to a Q&A for “Into th
body:
On my last morning in Telluride, halfway through breakfast at Butcher & Baker, Kenneth Branagh stopped at the table on his way to a Q&A for “Into the Breach,” the National Theatre documentary he produced. He had a story. A night earlier, he’d ridden the gondola up in pitch darkness with Willem Dafoe, Tom Hiddleston and Andrew Scott — four of the best actors alive, each with a film at the festival, sealed in one cable car with nothing to look at and nothing to do but talk. All anyone could hear was Dafoe. Branagh, laughing, called it “the wisdom of Willem.” A voice in the dark, no face attached.
	

	I half-believed it until a few hours later, waiting out my flight at Montrose, when I ran into Hiddleston on his way back to the U.K. He told the same story, unprompted.


	That’s the festival. The Telluriders have gone home, Venice wraps in a few days and we came down the mountain knowing more about this Oscar race than we did going up. Christopher Nolan’s mythological epic “The Odyssey” is still the one to beat. It won’t be a cakewalk. Here’s what else I carried down.



	

	



	“The Debut” handed Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti their moment.

	Jesse Eisenberg’s third feature behind the camera premiered Saturday night. By the next day, it was the hottest ticket in town. “The Debut” drops Moore’s Mona, a meek suburban homemaker who lands a bit part in a community theater musical, into the front of the best actress race. It’s the funniest, warmest thing she’s done in years. Giamatti, whom Eisenberg calls his “favorite actor,” plays the tyrant director shaping her. During one rehearsal scene between them — a master-class, no other word for it — the Telluride crowd applauded in the middle of the movie. You rarely see that happen once at a festival. It happened again before the credits.
	

	Moore already has an Oscar for “Still Alice,” and she’s the one to beat. Giamatti is the sentimental story coming up underneath: twice nominated for “Cinderella Man” and “The Holdovers,” never a winner and here he is doing the loosest work of his late career in a supporting turn built to be embraced. Eisenberg wrote seven songs for the fictional show. The one they’ll push is “This City May Have Chewed Me Up (But It Hasn’t Spit Me Out),” which Moore performs, and it’s headed for a best original song campaign.



	

					Nathan Fielder in “You Can See Everything”
									A24
	



	Nathan Fielder attempts the impossible.

	The festival’s best-kept secret came Sunday night, when ticket holders filed into the Werner Herzog Theatre with their phones locked away for “You Can See Everything,” the Elizabeth Holmes documentary Fielder co-directed with Lance Oppenheim, whose narrative feature “Primetime” premiered in Venice a day earlier. Holmes invites Fielder and his skeptical crew to film her in the 34 days before she reports to prison. The shoot spirals into a three-year descent. Portions are recreated with an A-list actor who is eligible for Oscar attention, though not SAG.

	Now comes the hard part, which is the documentary branch, which has never embraced this kind of nonfiction filmmaking. Voters who prize the observational and the sincere tend to bristle at a movie where the filmmaker is this present and this implicated. The circus around Fielder guarantees the kind of coverage most nonfiction contenders would trade a lung for. Whether the branch rewards it is the whole question. Nobody has made a movie quite like this. Almost nobody has won an Oscar for one.



	

					Jordan Firstman in “Club Kid”
									A24
	



	“Club Kid” has a real play for the old guard.

	Jordan Firstman’s directorial debut had its North American premiere Friday, and its trajectory keeps getting more serious than anyone bet on. Firstman writes, directs and stars as Peter, a washed-up New York party promoter whose life on the dance floor stops cold when the 10-year-old son he never knew about (British newcomer Reggie Absolom) turns up at his door.

	Strip away the club scene and the online-comedian brand, and you have a classically built story about a man-child being handed a kid. I expected that this would struggle to appeal to the older industry demographic. I was wrong. In fact, it seems to register incredibly well with older Academy voters, at least the ones I chatted with on the mountain.
	

	Veteran actor Colleen Camp, who first came to the festival in 1977, made the case for the film’s tonal control better than any campaign deck could. “I always say, always hire somebody funny to do something dramatic, because you’ll get so many interesting things,” she said at the post-screening Q&A. “And what [Firstman] did in this movie is even in the most dramatic moments, they’re brilliantly ironic and they’re funny.”

	Firstman described how his script reversed course on him over two years of writing. “I started the script from kind of a cynical place of looking around at the scene and just not feeling good about it — looking at the excessive drug use and the sex, and being a part of it and feeling bad about myself and feeling bad about my community,” he said. “What happened was that making this film in the community — we shot at real parties, in the queer spaces in New York — my empathy really opened up in the production of the film.” That shift is on the screen, and it’s what voters will feel without necessarily being able to name it.

	By the end of the panel, it came down to one word, spoken loudly by Firstman: “love.”



	

					L.A. BOLA NEGRA. Guitarricadelafuente as Sebastián in La Bola Negra. Cr. Carla Oset/Netflix © 2026.
									‘La Bola Negra’   Carla Oset/Netflix
	



	“La Bola Negra” commands the room.

	Respect is the currency at that altitude, and Los Javis have it. Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi arrived off a Cannes run that ended with the directing prize, and the Telluride word-of-mouth only got louder. Chris Pine, Sofia Coppola, Rian Johnson and their Netflix stablemate Danny Boyle (“Ink”) all turned up for the screening.

	Shot on 35 mm and inspired by the unfinished Federico García Lorca work of the same name, “La Bola Negra” moves across 1932, 1937 and 2017, tracing three generations of gay men through nearly a century of Spanish history.

	A subtitled Netflix title the festival can’t stop buzzing about is exactly where you want to be heading into the international feature race, and the streamer is hunting well beyond that category. And even though stars Guitarricadelafuente and Penélope Cruz weren’t on the mountain, the film played so well that it shows it can exist in the awards echo chamber without them (which says a lot).
	



	

					“Wild Horse Nine”
									Searchlight Pictures
	



	“Wild Horse Nine” made the two-stop drop look easy.

	Of the titles that ran the Venice-to-Telluride relay this year, Martin McDonagh’s landed with the most confidence. Searchlight Pictures’ “Wild Horse Nine” bowed in Venice competition on Sept. 3 to a 13-minute standing ovation, the Lido’s first real roar of the fall. Two days later, it turned up as Telluride’s surprise patron screening, timed to John Malkovich’s Silver Medallion tribute.

	Malkovich was the biggest takeaway. Twice nominated and never a winner, he called the script the kind you see “every 25 years.” The double premiere vaulted him near the front of best actor, trailing only Matt Damon in “The Odyssey” and another Telluride player, Andrew Scott in “Elsinore.” Sam Rockwell, who won supporting actor for his last McDonagh outing, is back in that conversation, with the open question of whether Steve Buscemi joins him.



	

					Kate O’Flynn, Paul Jesson and Marion Bailey in “Tender Loving Care”
									Thin Man Films Ltd and Bleecker Street
	



	“Tender Loving Care” is Mike Leigh in a minor key, and it wrecks you anyway.

	If this is the last Mike Leigh film, and the final shot plays like a man who knows it might be, it’s a hell of a way to leave. “Tender Loving Care” follows two social workers and was built the usual Leigh way: no script, no plot, just months of assembling people until they exist.

	Marion Bailey, who plays Birdie, figured out the assignment before the assignment existed. “I could see as he was going through, he was crossing off people and I thought, what’s the sort of person he’s looking for? And then it dawned on me — he’s looking for someone who has a sense of humor,” she said. “The ones he was crossing off my list were people who don’t have a sense of humor.” Then she added the part only a Leigh veteran gets to add: “You get a call from Mike to say, ‘Do you want to come on board? I don’t know what the part will be. I’m not sure how it’ll work out, but would you like to do it?’ Yes, please. You don’t even stop to think about it.”

	The film’s dedication to Dick Pope hangs over it, and longtime producer Georgina Lowe explained how the succession happened. Lucy, who came up under Pope as a camera trainee on “Meantime” and operated on “Hard Truths,” took over the cinematography after a British Society of Cinematographers function where Pope received a posthumous lifetime achievement award. “I don’t think Mike heard this, but Pat turned to Lucy and said, ‘You should shoot the next one,’” Lowe said. “Simultaneously, Mike had thought that. It just made total sense.”
	

	Paul Jesson gave the film its thesis in a single line, asking what a movie about caring for people means right now. “It’s also a good antidote to a world which, by and large, is being run by bullies and thugs,” he said. “The state of the world at the moment is pretty terrifying, really. A lot of people try to close their eyes, cover their ears and get on with their own private lives. And it’s hard to know what to do apart from that, other than look after the people they’re close to.” That’s the movie, and the campaign.



	

					Andrew Scott stars as Ian Charleson in ELSINORE, a Focus Features release.Credit: Anthony Dickenson / © 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLC
									Anthony Dickenson
	



	Everybody wrote a love letter to acting this year.

	Step back from the horse race and the weekend had a through-line: acting itself, in films made largely by and for the people who do it. Two of the marquee titles orbit the same building. “Elsinore” is Andrew Scott as Ian Charleson in the last year of his life, holding on long enough to play Hamlet at London’s National Theatre. “Into the Breach,” the documentary Branagh produced, tells the story of that same theater, with Judi Dench, Anthony Hopkins, Gary Oldman and Ian McKellen around a table sorting out what the stage cost them and what it gave back. One film stages a great actor’s final bow. The other rounds up living legends to explain why it mattered.

	“The Debut” is the same subject from the bottom of the ladder: Moore as a suburban nobody who discovers, in a community theater musical, that performing might be the truest thing she’s ever done and nearly comes apart proving it. A drama, a doc and a comedy, all circling what it costs to disappear into someone else.

	The actors branch is the largest bloc in the Academy, and nothing moves a room of performers like a film that treats performance as life or death. Telluride just handed them three.



	

	



	The gondola is the place to get honest polls.

	Nothing tells you how ticket holders are responding to a movie like a gondola ride to or from the Chuck Jones Theatre. On a ride up Sunday morning, you get to listen to the festival unfiltered, which, of course, came with the secret screening speculation that swung from a Frank Ocean project to the eventual Fielder documentary. But then you get to hear about people’s reactions to the Bill Gates talk at Elks Park that half the car caught the tail end of, and the running argument over which “Martin McDonagh is the real Martin McDonagh.” (Whatever that means?)
	

	One producer I chatted with had the most useful read of the weekend on “La Bola Negra,” which he claimed everyone kept calling too long. “I felt that it was long, but I was never bored,” he said. “I was pretty engaged. It felt pretty robust the whole time.” That distinction can matter most. It’s not about whether voters check their watches, but whether they mind. Turns out they don’t.

	However, he was less forgiving elsewhere about “Fjord,” Cristian Mungiu’s Romanian Palme d’Or winner. “I didn’t think there was any character work between the two of them [Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve]. I didn’t get their relationship at all,” he said. “They got these incredible actors and it didn’t just match. I wanted to hear more about their beliefs. I wanted to get more into it, be challenged more. It left me a little cold.”

	Interestingly, I spoke to someone else immediately after getting off the gondola who said “Fjord” is the best thing they’ve seen this year.

	The pendulum can swing rapidly between voters and titles.



	

	



	Other notes from the mountain

	Stephen Beresford, who wrote “Elsinore,” lost his passport and couldn’t make it to Telluride. That didn’t stop his leading man from having a moment.

	Andrew Scott had company for that reaction. After the screening, Oprah Winfrey, a Telluride regular this year behind Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s “Everest: The Other Side,” found Scott outside and cried in his arms. If you want to know how a movie is landing on the mountain, watch for who’s weeping in the lobby or outside.

	(That’s also “A Long Winter” writer and director Andrew Haigh weeping alongside them)

	Winfrey also threw a party, and by the chatter, all anyone could talk about was who got the invite, who didn’t and how you could possibly get one. Spoiler alert: I wasn’t one of them.

schema.headline: Telluride Takeaways: From Julianne Moore and Paul Giamatti’s ‘Debut’ to Nathan Fielder’s Audacious Dare to the Doc Branch

title: African American Film Critics Association Donates $25,000 to Black Film Hall of Fame – Film News in Brief
description:
The African American Film Critics Association (AAFCA) is donating $25,000 to the Black Film Hall of Fame. 

	“Supporting the Black Film Hall of Fame
body:
The African American Film Critics Association (AAFCA) is donating $25,000 to the Black Film Hall of Fame. 

	“Supporting the Black Film Hall of Fame with this modest gift fits perfectly with ourorganization’s goals to align with institutions that serve to preserve Black storytelling content,” AAFCA President Gil Robertson IV said in a statement.

	Founded in 2003, the Kansas City, Missouri-based museum and multicultural cultural center aims to preserve and celebrate Black cinema. The AAFCA is the largest collective of Black film critics in the world, and presents annual awards celebrations and special events that honor outstanding achievements in the entertainment industry.
	

	“The Black Movie Hall of Fame is beyond thrilled by the generosity of Gil Robertson and AFFCA,” executive director and film critic Shawn Edwards said in a statement. “It’s a natural partnership as AAFCA and its roster of film critics represent one of the least talked about but most important aspects when acknowledging the history of Black cinema. For decades, Black film critics championed Black movies at a time when they were largely overlooked by the mainstream press. We look forward to building a lasting relationship with AAFCA and its membership.” 

	
		‘Donnie Darko’ Returns to Theaters for 25th Anniversary	

	Fathom Entertainment and Saga Arts are bringing “Donnie Darko” back to theaters in new 4K restoration on Oct. 2-4.

	Beginning on “Donnie Darko Day,” the date in 1988 when the strange events of the film begin, the cult classic returns in its widest theatrical release for its 25th anniversary.
	

	Originally released in 2001, “Donnie Darko” stars Jake Gyllenhaal as the titular troubled teen who receives a mysterious warning of the impending end of the world. The star-studded supporting cast features Jena Malone, Drew Barrymore, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Mary McDonnell, Holmes Osborne, Noah Wyle, Patrick Swayze and Seth Rogen.

	The anniversary theatrical release also includes an exclusive introduction from writer and director Richard Kelly exploring the film’s legacy. The film was a box-office flop when it first premiered, but later found cult success in home video sales and reissues.

	Watch the special 25th anniversary trailer below.

            The owner of a Florida doggy daycare has been arrested after employees found a hidden camera in the bathroom.
      
    
            Dog Dayz Inn owner Donald Hemphill was charged after the camera was found inside an electrical outlet on Saturday.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            During the Volusia Sheriff's Office Child Exploitation Unit's investigation, Hemphill allegedly copped to installing the camera about 4 or 5 months ago.
      

            The VSO says multiple videos were found that showed unknowing female victims in "stages of undress." Authorities say one subject was a child.
      
    
            Hemphill has been charged with 10 counts of digital voyeurism and 11 counts of video voyeurism of a child.
      
    
            According to the Volusia Sheriff's Office Hemphill is being held without bond.
